html:
"Ainus" is the map's label, from 1279 to 1500, for the Ainu, the native people of Hokkaido, Sakhalin and the Kuril Islands, in the centuries when their culture took its classic form.

By this time the Ainu lived from salmon fishing, deer hunting and gathering, and above all from trade. They sold furs, dried fish, hawks and eagle feathers to Japanese merchants for iron, lacquerware, rice and sake, and traded with peoples on the Amur River for Chinese silks and beads.

Two contacts mark these centuries:

  • In the north, Ainu on Sakhalin clashed with the Yuan Mongols, who sent expeditions from the 1260s to the 1280s and pressed them to pay tribute in furs. See Mongol invasions of Sakhalin.
  • In the south, Japanese traders and warriors, under the loose rule of the shoguns, set up bases on the tip of Hokkaido. In 1457 the chief Koshamain led the Ainu against them after a Japanese smith killed an Ainu youth, in Koshamain's War. The Kakizaki family, later the Matsumae, won it and became the masters of Japanese trade with the Ainu.
